impĕrītĭa (inp- ), ae, f. imperitus,
I.inexperience, ignorance, awkwardness (mostly post-Aug.; “not in Cic. or Cæs.): Jugurtha, cognita vanitate atque imperitia legati, subdolus ejus augere amentiam,” Sall. J. 38, 1 ; cf. id. ib. 85, 45: “plurimum Marius imperitia hostium confirmatus,” id. ib. 99, 1 ; cf.: “pugnam imperitia poscere,” Tac. A. 13, 36 : “juvenum,” id. ib. 13, 42 : “imperitia et rusticitas afferunt interim frigus,” Quint. 6, 1, 37 : “contra Circium serere, imperitia existimatur,” Plin. 17, 2, 2, § 21 : “rerum atque verborum imperitia, Gell. N. A. praef. § 12: nimia,” Gai. Inst. 2, 109 .—In plur.: “grammatico insolentiarum et imperitiarum pleno,” id. 7, 17
in lemm.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
